items.source: Simon White (Bloomberg) via The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: SOFR, not Treasuries, is the cleaner Fed trade
items.idea: Speculators are near record net short SOFR futures — a clean, directional bet — while headline Treasury shorts are distorted by the basis trade (futures shorts paired with long cash bonds). The market has priced ~22bp of tightening for this week's FOMC plus ~28bp more over the next two meetings. A hold, cautious hike, or one-and-done guidance forces a violent unwind of the crowded SOFR short; Treasuries still need fiscal supply, term premium and Japanese demand to all cooperate.
items.angle: This is a vol-trade setup ahead of the Warsh FOMC decision — the front end offers a cleaner binary than duration, and it pairs directly with the Goldman hike call below.
items.tweetA: Everyone's trying to trade the Fed through 10yr Treasuries. Wrong instrument. SOFR shorts are near record and clean — Treasury shorts are contaminated by the basis trade. One dovish surprise from Warsh and the front end rips while duration barely moves.
items.tweetB: The AI-slowdown-means-lower-rates trade has a sequencing problem: capex hasn't actually slowed, only the rhetoric has. SOFR doesn't need that whole chain to work — it just needs Warsh to deliver less than a crowded short already expects.

charts.desc: Two Bloomberg charts: combined asset-manager + leveraged-fund net Treasury futures positioning (shrinking short) vs. SOFR speculative net short (near record).

items.title: Physical crude is trading $25-30/bbl over the benchmark — the inventory buffer is running out
items.idea: Physical crude is pricing $25-30/bbl above benchmarks today because ex-China inventory is too thin for comfort. HFIR's late-August math: if Iran fully chokes the Oman lane, the non-China buffer lasts only 15-21 days. Oddly, Oman-lane flows have risen to ~15mb/d (Kpler, incl. Fujairah) even as Iran fires on ships daily — yet Chinese state oil majors are suddenly buying aggressively just 9 days before the September 24 Xi-Trump summit.
items.angle: The physical premium is the tell that futures pricing is lagging real supply-chain stress; the timing of Chinese buying right before the summit is the geopolitical wrinkle worth watching.
items.tweetA: Physical crude is trading $25-30 OVER the benchmark right now. That's not a headline risk premium — that's inventory actually running out. The futures market hasn't caught up to the physical market yet.
items.tweetB: China's state oil majors are buying like crude is scarce — 9 days before the Xi-Trump summit. Either they know something about a deal we don't, or they're front-running their own worst-case scenario. Both are tradeable.

items.title: ‘Luck’ is a repeatable process, not a trait — and it maps to network theory
items.idea: The framework: randomize your routine to widen your ‘surface area’ for chance encounters, prioritize weak ties over your inner circle (your closest 5 already know everything you know), and detach emotionally from outcomes by journaling actions instead of results. Concrete mechanism: a daily 3-sentence action journal reportedly cuts anxiety ~90% because anxiety is reframed as ‘insufficient work on the primary goal’ — a measurable, fixable state rather than a feeling.
items.angle: This is retail packaging of structural-hole network theory (weak ties carry novel information) and an exploration/exploitation heuristic — a useful lens for deal sourcing and idea generation, not just personal productivity.
items.tweetA: Networking research 101 dressed up as a lifestyle newsletter: your inner circle already knows everything you know. Your next real edge comes from weak ties — the 30 acquaintances you meet by varying your routine, not the 5 people you talk to every day.
items.tweetB: Anxiety, reframed: it's not a feeling, it's a KPI. It means you did too little on your #1 priority today. Track 3 sentences a day on what you actually did — not planned — and the emotional noise collapses because the metric is binary: did the work, or didn't.

items.title: Investors now model Anthropic at $120B ARR by December, $350B by end-2027 — already ahead of its own IPO deck
items.idea: Anthropic's Q2 revenue hit $11.5B, up 14x YoY, with an adjusted (ex-stock-comp) operating profit — its second straight profitable quarter. Investors are now modeling $120B annualized revenue by December 2026 (up from prior guesstimates of $100B) and roughly $350B by end-2027, nearly triple. That's already ahead of the company's own prior IPO-deck figure of $190-200B for 2028, a year later. Gross margin runs above 80% on inference before Amazon's distribution cut and training costs.
items.angle: Compare growth to real-world reference points to make the number legible, and flag that the company's own deck is already stale versus what investors are underwriting.
items.tweetA: Anthropic's own S-1 deck says $190-200B revenue... for 2028. Investors are now underwriting $350B for 2027 — a year early and nearly double the company's own number. Someone's wrong, and normally it's whoever wrote the smaller number.
items.tweetB: 80%+ gross margin, but that's margin on inference BEFORE Amazon's distribution cut and training costs. 'Adjusted operating income positive' excludes stock comp at a company hiring flat out. Read the gross-vs-net line in the S-1 before you anchor on any of these figures.

items.title: Anthropic picks Nasdaq — the same passive-index trick SpaceX/xAI just ran
items.idea: Anthropic chose Nasdaq for its IPO listing, following SpaceX/xAI's playbook there earlier this year at a $1.75T valuation — a venue choice that historically can accelerate entry into the Nasdaq-100 and force passive-index buying of a low-float IPO. October remains the target, a $2T valuation is under discussion but not finalized, and Anthropic must release financials at least 15 days before the roadshow — meaning the public S-1 is likely days, not weeks, away.
items.angle: The exchange choice is itself a signal of the mechanical demand play being engineered — same setup as SpaceX/xAI.
items.tweetA: Anthropic didn't pick Nasdaq by accident. SpaceX/xAI did the same thing earlier this year and it turbocharged forced passive buying via Nasdaq-100 inclusion. A low-float, $2T IPO landing in a passive index is a liquidity event most public investors haven't priced in yet.
items.tweetB: 15-day disclosure rule + October IPO target = the S-1 is coming within days, not weeks. If you're waiting for 'more clarity' on Anthropic before positioning, the clarity window is closing faster than the market thinks.

items.title: Anthropic's penny-option compute deal flips the Nvidia circular-deal playbook
items.idea: Anthropic signed a $13.7B, six-year compute deal with Rum Group (formerly Rumble, hosts Truth Social; Thiel/Vance early investors) for a Georgia data-center site that isn't built and that Rum itself says it can't yet finance. In exchange, Anthropic gets options on 51 million Rum shares at one cent each versus a $7.17 stock price and $2.8B market cap, vesting on how much compute Anthropic actually buys.
items.angle: This is the Nvidia-style circular/boomerang financing pattern in reverse — the compute buyer, not the seller, holds the equity kicker, while underwriting a supplier that hasn't built the plant or secured financing.
items.tweetA: Anthropic just got options on 51M shares of a Trump-linked neocloud at a penny each — for a data center that isn't built, from a supplier that admits it doesn't have the financing. This is the Nvidia circular-deal playbook, except now the CUSTOMER holds the equity kicker.
items.tweetB: $13.7B committed to unbuilt capacity from an unfinanced counterparty, with political ties (Thiel, Vance) baked in. If this is what 'pacing the frontier' looks like from the demand side, the pace is fine — it's the balance sheet risk that's compounding.

items.title: ‘Pacing the frontier’ and protecting the IPO margin story are the same memo
items.idea: The FT reporting states plainly that slowing model releases saves Anthropic ‘billions in training costs’ while letting rivals close the gap — training costs are exactly what sits between the 80% inference margin and the actual operating line. Parekh's read: the public safety pause and the second consecutive profitable quarter are ‘the same decision, seen from two sides.’ David Sacks separately argued that trading raw capability for reliability, post-Hugging-Face-breach, is simply good business.
items.angle: Skepticism angle — the safety framing conveniently coincides with a margin need right before the IPO roadshow.
items.tweetA: Dario Amodei asks the industry to slow down on Saturday. By Sunday night Anthropic has two profitable quarters, a Nasdaq listing, and a new $13.7B compute deal. 'Pacing the frontier' and 'protecting the IPO margin story' are the same memo.
items.tweetB: Training costs are exactly what sits between Anthropic's 80% inference margin and its actual operating line. Every paused month of model development is a month the roadshow deck gets to call profit. Read the safety essay with that math in the same paragraph.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom (Goldman Sachs / Albert Edwards, SocGen)
items.title: Goldman now expects a September hike — to appease the market, not the economy
items.idea: Goldman's inflation and growth views haven't changed, yet it now expects a 25bp September hike — driven by fear of disappointing an already near-fully-priced market and destabilizing long-end yields, not by data. Albert Edwards (SocGen) counters that hiking while core inflation ex-shelter sits near 2% and wages cool repeats the ECB's July 2008 mistake: tightening into a growth air pocket just as an energy shock is already doing growth's job.
items.angle: Pairs directly with the SOFR trade above — same FOMC event, and flags the credibility framing (Warsh validating the market vs. confronting Trump).
items.tweetA: Goldman's own inflation and growth forecasts haven't changed. They added a hike anyway — because the market already priced it and they're scared of what happens to the long end if the Fed disappoints. That's a Fed capitulating to positioning, not to data.
items.tweetB: Albert Edwards is calling this the ECB's July 2008 mistake in real time: hike into decelerating core inflation and cooling wages, right as an energy shock is already doing growth's job for you. The ECB hiked a month before Lehman. Worth sitting with.

items.title: 10yr yield hit 5% and blinked — but ex-energy inflation is the lowest since early 2021
items.idea: The 10yr Treasury yield touched 5% and immediately reversed — a 'Blink,' not a 'Tip' (Authers' framing). The Fed funds terminal rate has been repriced up a full 50bp since Chair Warsh's Jackson Hole speech alone. Meanwhile inflation excluding energy was 2.5% last month, the lowest since early 2021 — meaning the entire move is an energy-shock-plus-Fed-credibility story, not a broad inflation story.
items.angle: Separate the real driver (Iran/energy + Fed reaction function) from what headlines will call it (inflation fear) — useful for framing the FOMC reaction Wednesday.
items.tweetA: 10yr hit 5%, and traders immediately took it back — a blink, not a tip. But look at what's actually moving: ex-energy inflation is the lowest since early 2021. This isn't an inflation selloff, it's an oil-shock-plus-Fed-credibility selloff wearing an inflation costume.
items.tweetB: Warsh's Jackson Hole speech alone added 50bp to the priced terminal rate. The market isn't pricing the data, it's pricing Warsh's reaction function. That's a much less stable anchor than 'the Fed follows inflation' — and it can reprice on a single Wednesday statement.

charts.desc: Chart of Fed funds futures repricing (from 3.5% actual to ~4.5% implied terminal by next summer) since Jackson Hole.

items.source: John Authers (Bloomberg Points of Return, w/ Michael Howell, Jim Reid, LPL Financial)
items.title: The base rate says don't panic: stocks were higher a year into 5 of the last 6 Fed hiking cycles
items.idea: Ex-pandemic distortions, nominal GDP growth is running near its fastest pace since the 1980s (Michael Howell chart), which correlates historically with rising 10yr yields. Jim Reid's (Deutsche Bank) historical framework puts the 10yr at 6% before this hiking cycle is done. LPL's chart of S&P performance after the last six Fed hiking cycles shows equities almost always higher a year in — 2022 (Fed starting far behind the curve) is the lone exception, and March 1997 (one-and-done) the lone outlier the other way.
items.angle: Challenge the reflexive 'hikes = bad for stocks' assumption using the base rate, while flagging the one scenario (behind-the-curve hiking) that actually breaks it.
items.tweetA: Base rate check: in 5 of the last 6 Fed hiking cycles, the S&P was HIGHER a year later. The one exception was 2022, when the Fed started miles behind the curve. If Warsh hikes now, ahead of a growth air pocket rather than behind it, the base rate says don't panic-sell equities.
items.tweetB: Nominal GDP growth is running near its fastest pace since the 1980s once you strip out pandemic distortions. Rate hikes into strong nominal growth aren't a crisis signal — they're what the data is supposed to produce. The market is trading this like 2022 when the chart says otherwise.

charts.desc: Michael Howell nominal-GDP-vs-10yr chart; Jim Reid historical tightening-cycle chart projecting a 6% 10yr; LPL Financial chart of S&P performance after the last six Fed hiking cycles (1997 and 2022 as the outliers).

items.source: John Authers (Bloomberg Points of Return, citing Noah Smith, BofA's Justin Post)
items.title: The AI-slowdown trade isn't risk-off — it's a rotation into software
items.idea: Frontier labs are stuck in a prisoner's dilemma: each prefers coordinated deceleration but none will unilaterally slow for fear rivals keep going (Noah Smith's framing). Trump publicly called the safety push 'a SICK conspiracy.' The S&P 1500 software index rallied 3.2% Monday specifically because a real AI slowdown would be a lifeline for 'SaaSpocalypse' survivors being priced out by AI disruption; BofA's Justin Post flags $200B+ of Alphabet/Amazon revenue backlog tied to AI-lab spending that isn't fully funded yet.
items.angle: The trade isn't 'AI slowdown = bad for markets,' it's 'AI slowdown = sector rotation from infra/chips into software incumbents.'
items.tweetA: The AI-slowdown trade isn't risk-off. It's a rotation. Software just ripped 3.2% in one day because a slower AI pace is the best thing that could happen to the companies AI was supposed to kill. Long the 'SaaSpocalypse' survivors, not the panic.
items.tweetB: Noah Smith's point cuts deeper than people are using it: these labs are calling for a slowdown AGAINST their own financial interest, in a textbook prisoner's dilemma where cooperation only works if nobody free-rides. That's either the most sincere risk signal in tech history, or the best-timed one right before two mega-IPOs.

charts.desc: Chart contrasting the S&P 1500 software index's 3.2% Monday rally against the chipmaker selloff.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom (Goldman Sachs Oil Tracker / Yulia Zhestkova Grigsby)
items.title: Saudi 'resilience' is really concentration risk — the system is out of spare lanes
items.idea: Saudi exports recovered to June levels purely through rerouting — shifting away from the Red Sea back through eastern ports — after its 7mb/d East-West pipeline closed. That's less redundancy, not more resilience. August's oil balance deteriorated to roughly a 3mb/d deficit. Two remaining shock absorbers, slower SPR releases and China staying on the sidelines, are both about to flip against the market at once. Options price a 44% probability that February Brent expires above $100/bbl.
items.angle: The rerouting story is being read by the market as resilience when it's actually the system using up its last spare lane — one more infrastructure hit and there's nowhere left to reroute.
items.tweetA: Saudi exports 'held' at June levels — but only because they rerouted through eastern ports after a 7mb/d pipeline shut down. That's not resilience, that's using up the last spare lane. One more infrastructure hit and there's nowhere left to reroute to.
items.tweetB: Two of the oil market's remaining shock absorbers — SPR releases and paused Chinese buying — are both about to flip against the market at the same time, right as August already ran a 3mb/d deficit. 44% odds on Feb Brent above $100 looks cheap against that setup. $XLE $USO

items.title: An AI-extinction resignation reached a 76-year-old grandmother within days
items.idea: A 27-year-old Anthropic researcher publicly resigned warning of AI extinction risk; within days the story propagated far enough that a caller's 76-year-old mother was texting her in a panic — mainstream, non-tech-literate audience anxiety, not just AI-Twitter discourse. Jason Calacanis pushes back that the labs are already shipping the safeguards the 'doomer' narrative claims don't exist.
items.angle: The propagation speed into a demographic that never engages with AI-safety discourse is the real leading indicator here — for political/regulatory pressure, not for a market signal per se.
items.tweetA: The AI-extinction story didn't stay in AI Twitter. It reached a 76-year-old grandmother in under a week. That propagation speed into non-tech demographics is the actual leading indicator for regulatory backlash — not the resignation letter itself.
items.tweetB: Every 'AI safety researcher quits in warning' story this month has landed within days of a mega-IPO pricing update. Not saying it's coordinated. Saying the market should price the correlation, not just the content.

items.title: Weed farms as data centers: the power-constraint arbitrage has gotten this specific
items.idea: A caller asked whether a 1.5-3 megawatt cannabis cultivation facility could be converted into a data center — grow-op infrastructure (high-density power delivery, climate control, security, an existing grid interconnect) is structurally similar to small-scale AI compute siting, and is being scouted as real-estate arbitrage wherever power-constrained compute demand can find a pre-built, grid-connected shell.
items.angle: A small but telling data point on how far the power-constraint arbitrage has spread — any non-traditional industrial real estate with a grid connection is now compute-site inventory.
items.tweetA: The data center power hunt has gotten weird enough that people are seriously asking if cannabis grow facilities can become AI compute sites. Same power density, same climate control, same 'already has the grid interconnect' scarcity value. Watch this pattern spread to any pre-built industrial shell.
items.tweetB: Every power-constrained AI compute story eventually becomes a real estate story. If a 1.5-3MW weed farm has scarcity value purely because of its grid connection, that tells you how tight interconnection queues actually are — tighter than chip supply in a lot of regions.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom (Goldman Sachs / Tony Pasquariello)
items.title: 27 straight sub-1% sessions isn't calm — it's 0DTE options mechanically pinning the tape
items.idea: The S&P has gone 27 consecutive sessions with an intraday range below 1%. Goldman's Tony Pasquariello frames that calm as mechanical — driven by the growing influence of zero-day-to-expiry (0DTE) options volatility harvesting in a low-volume market, not by genuine calm underneath. Positioning is no longer euphoric, meaning September/October could still deliver corrective pressure even from this base, but reduced discretionary exposure could leave a better technical setup heading into year-end.
items.angle: Distinguish 'low realized vol' from 'low risk' — 0DTE flow compresses the tape mechanically, so the calm can break suddenly without any new fundamental catalyst.
items.tweetA: 27 straight sessions with intraday range under 1% isn't calm — it's 0DTE options flow mechanically pinning the tape in low volume. That kind of compression doesn't resolve gently. When it breaks, it gaps, because there was never real price discovery underneath it.
items.tweetB: Positioning is no longer euphoric heading into a Fed decision and an oil shock. That's the bullish read buried in this piece: reduced discretionary exposure now could set up better technicals into year-end, even if the next few weeks are rough.

charts.desc: Likely chart of the S&P's 27-session intraday-range compression streak — worth opening.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom (Goldman Sachs / Rich Privorotsky)
items.title: The warning is the evidence: AI slowdown calls confirm the pace, not deny it
items.idea: Rich Privorotsky's counter-framing: warnings that AI development should slow down are themselves evidence of how fast capability is actually advancing — the warning and the acceleration are the same signal read two ways. This converges with two other items from the same window: the margin motive behind Anthropic's pause (item 7) and the labs' prisoner's-dilemma logic (item 11) — three unrelated desks, three different reasons, one shared conclusion: don't take the safety framing at face value.
items.angle: Cross-source convergence is itself the signal — when three unrelated analysts land on the same skepticism from three different angles in one 6-hour window, that's the trade.
items.tweetA: Three different desks this week landed on the same skepticism from three different angles: the safety pause protects margins (Parekh), it's a prisoner's dilemma nobody can unilaterally exit (Smith/Authers), and the warning itself proves the capability jump is real (Privorotsky). When three unrelated analysts converge on 'don't take this at face value,' that's the trade.
items.tweetB: If AI weren't actually accelerating, nobody would bother warning about it. The existence of the warning is Bayesian evidence against the 'AI is plateauing' bear case, not for it.
